<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par117 />according to ''q'', mostly take an intensifying attribute. On the other hand, they must not be regarded as adverbial (instrumental) accusatives, nor are they to be classed with the second (neuter) subjects treated below in {{GHGpar|144|l}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|t}}
Examples of the accusative following the verb are {{GHGheb|text=וָֽאֶזְעַק קֽוֹל־גָּדוֹל|translate=and I cried a loud voice}}, i.e. with a loud voice, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=11|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=23}} (after the proper object, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=5|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=8|verse=55}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=109|verse=2}} ''they have spoken unto me'' {{GHGheb|text=לְשׁוֹן שֶׁ֫קֶר|translate=a tongue of deceit}}, i.e. with a lying tongue; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=10|verse=4}} ''he'' becometh ''poor'' {{GHGheb|text=עשֶֹׁה כַף־רְמִיְּה|translate=dealing a slack hand}}, i.e. who dealeth with a slack hand; cf. the German ''eine schöne Stimme singen'', to sing a fine voice, ''eine tüchtige Klinge schlagen'', to smite a trusty sword, ''Schlittschuhe laufen'', to run skates (i.e. to skate), and our ''to write a good hand, to play ball'', &c.—Examples of the accusative preceding are {{GHGheb|text=שִֹׂפְתֵי רְנָנוֹת יְהַלֶּל־פִּי|translate=my mouth shall praise}} with ''joyful lips'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=63|verse=6}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=12|verse=3}}, where a ''casus instrumenti'' with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}} follows the accusative.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|u}}
'''4.''' Many verbs originally intransitive (sometimes even in form; see a, note 2 may be used also as transitives, in consequence of a certain modification of their original meaning, which has gradually become established by usage; cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=רִיב|translate=to strive}}, but also with an accusative ''causam alicuius agere'' (so even in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=17}}, &c.; elsewhere with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}} of the person for whom one strives); {{GHGheb|text=יָכֹל}} absolutely ''to be able'', with an accusative ''to prevail over'' any one; {{GHGheb|text=חָפֵץ|translate=to be inclined}} and {{GHGheb|text=רָצָה|translate=to have pleasure}} (usually with {{GHGheb|text=בְּ}}), with an accusative to ''wish for some one'' or ''something''; {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכַב|translate=cubare}}, then in the sense of ''concumbere'', originally joined with {{GHGheb|text=עִם־|translate=cum}}, but quite early also with the accusative, equivalent to ''comprimere'' (''feminam''), &c. So in {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=13|verse=14}}, &c., unless in all or some of the passages the preposition {{GHGheb|text=אֵת}} is intended, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אִתָּהּ}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֹתָהּ}}; in the earlier passages {{GHGheb|text=עִם־}} is the more usual.

{{GHGmargin-letter|117|v}}
Rem. 1. It is certainly difficult to decide whether some verbs, which were afterwards used absolutely or joined with prepositions, were not nevertheless originally ''transitive'', and consequently it is only the supposed original meaning, usually assigned to them in English, which causes them to appear ''intransitive''.<ref>Thus e.g. {{GHGheb|text=עָנָה|translate=to reply to}} (ἀμείβεσθαί τινα), ''to answer any one''; {{GHGheb|text=צִוָּה|translate=to command}} (iubere aliquem); {{GHGheb|text=זָכַר|translate=to remember}}; {{GHGheb|text=קִוָּה}} (also with {{GHGheb|text=לְ}}) ''to wait for any one'' (to expect any one); {{GHGheb|text=בִּשַֹׂר|translate=to bring glad tidings to any one}} (see the Lexicon); {{GHGheb|text=נָאַף}} and {{GHGheb|text=נִאֵף|translate=to commit adultery}} (adulterare matronam); {{GHGheb|text=עָבַד|translate=to serve}} (colere); {{GHGheb|text=עָרַב|translate=to become surety for}} ..., and many others.</ref> In that case there is of course no syntactical peculiarity to be considered, and a list of such verbs would at the most be requisite only for practical purposes. Moreover, it is also possible that certain verbs were originally in use at the same time both as transitive and intransitive, e.g. perhaps {{GHGheb|text=לָבֵשׁ|translate=to be clothed}} along with {{GHGheb|text=לָבַשׁ|translate=to put on}} (a garment). Finally the analogy of certain transitives in constant use may have led to intransitives of kindred meaning being also united directly with the accusative, so that, in other words, whole classes of verbs came to be regarded in a particular aspect as transitives. See below, y.<section end=par117 /><noinclude>
